To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the most common approach to priority setting in healthcare is a top-down approach; (2) there is no clear evidence that priority setting in healthcare should be done by a single decision maker, or by a committee or a group; (3) there is a lack of empirical evidence on whether or not the process of priority setting in healthcare can be fair; (4) priority setting in healthcare may be done in a way that is fair, and that is in the best interests of patients

the majority of people in our sample (i) believe that priority-setting is important, (ii) believe that it is the responsibility of healthcare providers, (iii) believe that it should involve patients and the public in the decision-making process, and (iv) believe that it needs to be fair.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how priority-setting decisions are made and whether they are fair.
how the NHS makes choices about which treatments to offer to which patients, and how these decisions should be made.
the process of priority setting for health care.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current system is not equitable, efficient and effective, and that it is not sustainable in the long run.

the priority-setting process is a complex, multi-dimensional process that is not only influenced by the political and economic climate but also the social and cultural environment in which the process is taking place.
there is no one best method for priority-setting, as the best method depends on the specific context and the goals of the priority-setting process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the current system of priority-setting in the Swedish health care system is fair, but that the system is not optimal.
we found that the majority of priority setting processes in low and middle-income countries were fair.
priority setting is not a technical issue, but a social and political process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a lot more to be done to ensure that the voices of patients and the public are heard in the priority-setting process.
the public is not well served by the current process for setting health priorities in Ontario.

, in the context of a health system that is already underfunded and underresourced, it is important to ensure that priority setting is done fairly, in a transparent and participatory way, to avoid unintended consequences and to promote the equitable use of scarce resources.
